messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 60

**Patient: Mr. A., 64-year-old married South Asian male, warehouse worker.**

Mr. A. came to see me at the urging of his youngest son, who told him he was “not the same father anymore.” He sits heavily in the chair, his hands resting on his knees, calloused and still bearing the faint blue stain of ink from a shipping label that didn’t come off. He speaks slowly, carefully, as if testing the weight of each word before letting it fall.

He was 28 years old, living in a small city in Gujarat, working as a clerk for a textile exporter. He was not a political man. He was a husband of two years, a new father. One evening, he was walking home from the chai stall when a van pulled up beside him. Men he did not recognize pulled him inside. He thought it was a robbery. It was not a robbery.

For 18 days, he was held in a windowless room. He never learned who his captors were, or why they chose him. They spoke in clipped, angry sentences. They wanted money from his employer, he later understood. He was beaten, starved, and kept in a space so small he could not fully extend his legs. He was blindfolded for most of it, but he remembers the smell—damp concrete, rust, his own sweat and fear. He remembers the sound of a ceiling fan that clicked with every rotation, a metronome of terror. He learned to count the clicks to keep from screaming. He was released in a field at dawn, dumped out of the van like a sack of grain. He walked home. He did not tell his wife the full truth for thirty years.

Now, at 64, Mr. A. works the night shift at a distribution center. He prefers the dark. The warehouse is vast, filled with towering metal shelves and the hum of forklifts. He is responsible for scanning pallets and stacking boxes. The work is repetitive, physical, and quiet. He likes that no one talks to him. He has not taken a single sick day in twelve years. He cannot afford to stop moving.

But the ceiling fan in his bedroom—the one his wife insisted on installing for the summer heat—has become a problem. He cannot sleep under it. The click of the pull chain, the rhythmic rotation, it brings him back to that room. He now sleeps on a thin mattress on the floor of the living room, away from the fan. His wife thinks it is his back pain. He lets her think that.

He is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. At work, he stands with his back to the wall during his break. He cannot tolerate anyone approaching him from behind. When a young coworker once clapped him on the shoulder as a joke, Mr. A. spun around and shoved him against a shelf. He apologized profusely, but the shame has not left him. He now avoids the break room entirely.

He has not been able to enter a crowded market in years. The press of bodies, the noise, the inability to see the exits—it triggers a physical panic he cannot control. His heart pounds, his vision narrows, and he feels a cold certainty that he is about to be taken again. He leaves his grocery shopping to his wife. He tells himself it is a matter of efficiency.

He is irritable with his grandchildren. Their sudden noises, their unexpected touches, make him flinch. He has stopped attending family gatherings. He feels hollow, disconnected, as if he is watching his own life from behind a sheet of glass. He does not cry. He has not cried since the third day of his captivity, when he realized no one was coming.

He came to my office because his son said he was “scared of everything.” Mr. A. does not see it that way. He sees himself as a man who survived by being careful. He does not know that the war ended long ago, and that he is still living inside that room, counting the clicks of the fan.
